raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils, most commonly immunoglobulin light chain amyloid (AL) and transthyretin amyloid (ATTR) [1], [2]. AL results from a clonal plasma-cell disorder and is a hematologic emergency because circulating light chains are directly cardiotoxic; ATTR is caused either by age-related wild-type transthyretin misfolding or by pathogenic TTR variants [3], [4]. Recognition has accelerated because noninvasive imaging, biomarker staging, and disease-modifying therapies have changed cardiac amyloidosis from a rarely diagnosed “restrictive cardiomyopathy” to an actionable diagnosis [5], [6].

Epidemiology is phenotype-driven. Autopsy studies show wild-type ATTR deposits in a substantial proportion of very elderly people, but clinical disease remains underdiagnosed [7]. ATTR is now found among older patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, unexplained left ventricular wall thickening, atrial arrhythmias, carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, and severe aortic stenosis referred for valve intervention [8], [9]. Natural-history cohorts show that ATTRwt typically presents in older men with heart failure, atrial arrhythmias, conduction disease, and elevated natriuretic peptides, whereas hereditary ATTR varies by genotype and ancestry [28], [29], [30].

Diagnosis begins with suspicion. Red flags include increased ventricular wall thickness disproportionate to QRS voltage, apical-sparing longitudinal strain, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, thickened valves, pericardial effusion, neuropathy, nephrotic-range proteinuria, and a history of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. The first branching point is exclusion of AL: serum and urine immunofixation plus serum free light chains are mandatory, because a positive bone scan alone is insufficient when a monoclonal protein is present [10]. In patients without monoclonal gammopathy, grade 2–3 myocardial uptake on technetium-labeled bone scintigraphy can diagnose ATTR noninvasively [10]. DPD and PYP scintigraphy transformed practice by distinguishing ATTR from most AL cardiac amyloidosis [11], [12]. Echocardiographic strain supports suspicion but is not definitive [13]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance demonstrates characteristic late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal gadolinium kinetics, and expanded extracellular volume; native T1 mapping may detect early involvement, especially when contrast is undesirable [14], [15]. Tissue biopsy with amyloid typing by mass spectrometry remains essential when tests are discordant or AL cannot be excluded.

Risk stratification integrates biomarkers, renal function, functional capacity, and amyloid type. ATTR staging systems using NT-proBNP, troponin, and estimated glomerular filtration rate identify patients with sharply different survival [16]. In AL amyloidosis, cardiac biomarkers dominate prognosis; Mayo staging with troponin and NT-proBNP, later refined by serum free light-chain difference, guides urgency and treatment intensity [17], [18]. Hematologic and cardiac response criteria are clinically meaningful because rapid light-chain suppression can translate into organ stabilization or improvement [19].

Management is subtype-specific and multidisciplinary. AL therapy targets the plasma-cell clone; daratumumab combined with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone has become a key frontline regimen, improving deep hematologic responses [20]. Selected patients may receive autologous stem-cell transplantation, but advanced cardiac involvement increases risk. ATTR therapy aims to stabilize transthyretin or reduce hepatic TTR production. Tafamidis reduced mortality and cardiovascular hospitalization in ATTR-CM and established transthyretin stabilization as disease-modifying therapy [21]. Acoramidis, another stabilizer, improved a hierarchical composite including death, cardiovascular hospitalization, NT-proBNP, and 6-minute walk distance [22]. RNA silencers have expanded options: vutrisiran improved cardiovascular outcomes in ATTR-CM, while patisiran preserved functional capacity and quality of life in ATTR cardiac amyloidosis; earlier APOLLO cardiac analyses showed favorable effects on wall thickness and natriuretic peptides [23], [24], [25].

Supportive care remains crucial. Diuretics are the cornerstone for congestion, but hypotension, autonomic dysfunction, renal impairment, and small stroke volume limit conventional heart-failure drugs. Atrial fibrillation is common in ATTR and often poorly tolerated; rhythm-control strategies may be more effective earlier in disease [26]. Because atrial mechanical dysfunction creates thrombotic risk even with modest arrhythmia burden, anticoagulation is generally favored for atrial fibrillation irrespective of CHA₂DS₂-VASc, and transesophageal or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging should be considered before cardioversion [27]. Pacemakers are frequently required for conduction disease, whereas defibrillator benefit is individualized. The future of cardiac amyloidosis care will depend on earlier detection, genotype-informed family screening, combination therapy, and validated measures of amyloid regression.
